column4: Before Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh, Allah rejects their fear and says that He is with them, listening; it is a second direct assurance that the messengers will not be left alone.

This single retrospective ayah returns Moses to his mother, rescues him after the killing, keeps him for years among Midian's people, and brings him back according to measure, repeatedly turning exposure and departure into care.
Pharaoh's household picks the cast-away infant from the river; this is the first human reception of the child entrusted to the water, though the ayah also foretells later enmity and grief.
Pharaoh's wife calls Moses a comfort to the eye, forbids killing him, and proposes taking him as a son, converting the abandoned infant's arrival into household shelter.
After Moses refuses other nurses, his sister directs the household to a family who will care for him sincerely, the concrete means by which the deposited child is preserved and returned.
Jacob fears that the brothers will take Joseph away and that a wolf will eat him while they are heedless, directly joining departure to the danger of neglected care.
Joseph asks to be placed over the land's storehouses because he is a knowing guardian, making preservation of hidden provision an explicit office.
After the well, sale, and prison, Allah establishes Joseph in the land so he may settle wherever he wishes, answering successive displacements with secure residence.
After the cave's long preservation, the ayah says Allah best knows how long the youths remained and that they have no protector besides Him, joining duration to exclusive guardianship.
Lot wishes for power or a strong support to which he might take refuge, using the section's sheltering verb to name the protection his exposed household needs.
The emigrants who left homes and the believers who sheltered and helped them are made mutual protectors, turning departure into received communal care.
Those who believed and emigrated are again joined to those who sheltered and helped, and are named the true believers with provision assured.
Allah makes night a covering, sleep repose, and day a rising, expanding the settled-night image into enclosure, rest, and renewed departure.
Allah promises not to let any worker's work be lost and immediately includes those who emigrated and were expelled from their homes, preserving both persons and deeds through forced departure.
People expelled from homes unjustly are placed under Allah's defense, and the ayah promises that He surely supports those who support Him.
Lot's people answer his warning by demanding that his household be expelled from the town, staging communal rejection as literal removal.
Allah saves Lot and his household except his wife, answering the expulsion threat in 7:82 with selective divine rescue.
The only answer of Lot's people is again to order his family expelled, because they are people who keep themselves pure.
Allah then saves Lot and his family except the wife whose remaining with the condemned is decreed.
The angels assure Lot that his enemies will not reach him and command a protected night departure with his family, while specifying the boundary represented by his wife.
Lot is told to travel with his family during part of the night, follow behind them, and let none turn back, making departure itself the divinely guarded route of rescue.
Noah is told to place paired creatures and his family in the ark when the flood begins, so threatened lives are gathered into a protective vessel.
Noah's prayer asks his Lord to bring him to a blessed landing and names Him the best giver of lodging, explicitly entrusting the end of the voyage to divine settlement.
Noah calls his separated son to board with the family and not remain with the unbelievers, supplying the offered refuge that the son refuses in 11:43.
The Prophet is told to wait patiently for his Lord's judgment and not be like Jonah when he called out in distress, introducing a messenger who left and nevertheless remained within divine response.
The ayah says that without favor overtaking Jonah he would have been cast blameworthy onto the bare shore, making divine grace the intervention against discarded exposure.
Jonah's Lord then chooses him and makes him one of the righteous, completing the movement from flight and casting-out to restored election.
Jonah's own glorification is named as the condition that precedes his release from the fish, showing relation with Allah persisting inside confinement.
The counterfactual says Jonah would have remained in the fish until resurrection, turning “remaining” into the fate from which divine response releases him.
Allah casts the sick Jonah onto the open shore, a scene of apparent disposal whose protective continuation comes in 37:146.
Allah grows a broad-leaved plant over Jonah, placing cover and care directly over the exposed body on the shore.
Jonah goes away in anger, then calls from layered darkness and confesses; the scene tests the thought that departure could put him beyond his Lord's power or hearing.
Allah answers Jonah, rescues him from distress, and generalizes that rescue to believers, explicitly resolving the departure-and-darkness scene.
Pharaoh recalls that Moses was raised in his household as a child and remained there for years, a true sheltering history voiced as a hostile claim of ownership.
Moses is commanded to leave by night with Allah's servants and make a dry sea path without fear of being overtaken, a departure whose way is prepared and guarded.
The flood vessel or its story is left as a sign for remembrance, making what is left behind something intentionally preserved rather than discarded.
Humans return to Allah alone and leave behind everything He had bestowed, sharply distinguishing the departing person from possessions that cannot accompany or keep them.
After Noah's rescue, Allah makes his descendants the survivors, so the flood narrative identifies who is made to remain.
Allah leaves Noah's honored remembrance among later generations, an explicit instance of leaving as preservation through time.
The same formula leaves Abraham's remembrance among later generations, repeating the positive sense of a legacy made to remain.
Moses and Aaron likewise have their remembrance left among later generations after rescue and support.
Elijah's remembrance is left among later generations, completing another repeated formulation of enduring honor.
Zakaria fears what will happen after he is gone while his wife is barren, so his request for an heir grows directly from anxiety about what departure leaves exposed.
He asks for an heir who will inherit from him and Jacob's house and be pleasing to the Lord, specifying the continuing relation sought in 19:5.
The oppressed ask their Lord to bring them out of a tyrannical town and appoint a protector and helper, joining needed departure to requested divine guardianship.
The magicians tell Pharaoh that Allah is better and more enduring, choosing the abiding Lord over a ruler's immediate threat.
The enduring good deeds are again said to be better with the Lord in reward and return, a repeated direct formulation of what remains.
The arrival of truth makes falsehood vanish because falsehood is inherently vanishing, a clear boundary between what remains and what cannot.
Allah effaces or confirms what He wills while the Mother of the Book remains with Him, directly juxtaposing removal and establishment under divine possession.
The ayah recalls that Allah and His Messenger enriched the people from divine bounty, another direct use of غ ن ي for granted sufficiency.
Poor prospective spouses are promised that Allah will enrich them from His bounty, repeating the transition from need to sufficiency.
The cloud held under command between heaven and earth presents the source dictionary's cloud object as suspended and sustained within divine ordering.
Satan strips Adam and his wife of their clothing to expose them, reversing the source dictionary's garment safely enclosed and the Qur'anic garment that covers.
Those who forget Allah are made to forget themselves, a moral consequence that clarifies the destructive form of forgetfulness against divine remembering care.
The one who deems himself self-sufficient uses the غ ن ي family for a false independence, reversing the sufficiency Allah grants to the needy.
The human transgresses because he sees himself self-sufficient, showing the corrupt counterfeit of the enrichment given by the Lord.
Abu Lahab's wealth does not avail him, using غ ن ي in the “benefit or suffice” sense to deny that possessions can provide lasting security.
The condemned speaker says his wealth did not avail him, another boundary showing that worldly sufficiency cannot keep its owner.
A person's wealth will not avail him when he falls, opposing stored wealth to the care that truly suffices.
The unbelievers are driven to Hell in groups, directly realizing the “drive and lead” action in the source explanation of قَلَىٰ as punitive expulsion.
The God-fearing are also led in groups, but to the Garden, showing that being driven onward can end in reception rather than rejection.
The guilty are driven thirsty to Hell, another direct occurrence of the source dictionary's leading-away action with an openly punitive destination.
The ayah addresses orphan women denied what was prescribed for them, a specific institutional form of the neglected care evoked by يَتِيم.
Fear of failing justice toward orphan girls governs the marriage instruction, exposing how guardianship can become exploitation rather than protection.
The hostile people are recalled as having resolved to expel the Messenger, another specific attempt to force the Prophet away.
The enemies' expulsion of the Messenger and believers is named while believers are warned not to entrust affection to them.
The Prophet is addressed through the fate of towns stronger than the town that expelled him, placing his forced departure under a divine reversal.
The arrogant chiefs threaten to expel Shuayb and the believers unless they return to the old religion, a messenger-specific repetition of forced separation.
Allah tells the angels that He is with them and commands them to make the believers firm in battle, converting divine presence into concrete support.
Allah is said to be with people wherever they are and to see what they do, a universal statement of presence behind the section's personal reassurance.
If the hearers turn away, they are reminded that Allah is their protector and the best protector and helper.
Allah declares that He defends those who believe, supplying a general protection claim immediately before the expulsion scene of 22:40.
Believers who support Allah's cause are promised His support and the firming of their feet, a reciprocal form of not being left unsupported.
Noah is told to disembark with peace and blessings, completing the ark's temporary custody in a divinely secured new settlement.
When the water overflowed, Allah carried human forebears in the vessel, presenting the ark as collective safekeeping.
The descendants carried in the laden ship are made a sign, another compact picture of lives held and transported through danger.
Moses leaves the city fearful and watchful while asking his Lord for rescue, initiating a vulnerable departure that reaches safety in 28:25.
As Moses turns toward Midian he hopes his Lord will guide him to the right way, entrusting the route after flight to divine direction.
At the Midian household Moses is told not to fear because he has escaped the wrongdoing people, marking arrival at human shelter after flight.
The youths explain that discovery would mean stoning or forced return to unbelief, specifying the danger from which the cave keeps them.
The stated centuries of the youths' stay make the cave's protective duration explicit rather than merely implied.
Those unable to marry are told to remain chaste until Allah enriches them, placing patient need under anticipated divine sufficiency.
Believers who faithfully observe their trusts enact the keeper's side of the section's deposited-object relation.
The same description of guarding trusts and covenants repeats safekeeping as a defining faithful practice.
The noble Qur'an is identified as the precious object whose enclosing place is named in 56:78.
The Qur'an is located in a protected or hidden book, paralleling the source dictionary's valuable object enclosed for preservation.
David is taught to make armor that protects people from violence, another crafted covering whose function is safekeeping.
The secure womb-deposit of 77:21 is retained until a known measure, adding bounded duration to protected placement.
Human beings are formed in their mothers' wombs through darkness layered upon darkness, a hidden enclosure in which creation is kept through stages.
Spouses are called garments for one another, making covering and intimate mutual shelter a relational use of the garment image.
Clothing is given to cover nakedness and as adornment, stating the garment's protective-covering function before 7:27 stages its loss.
Truth is hurled against falsehood until it crushes it and falsehood vanishes, another active formulation of what cannot remain.
The present life is called play and diversion while the hereafter is the real life, distinguishing temporary appearance from enduring reality.
Allah leaves from Lot's destroyed town a clear sign for people who understand, making a remnant preserve the lesson of those who departed.
A sign is left in the same punished settlement for those who fear painful punishment, another purposeful remnant after destruction.
Pharaoh's people leave behind gardens and springs, showing possessions and dwellings remaining after their owners are forced away.
What Pharaoh's people leave is inherited by another people, clarifying that departure changes custody rather than making the goods disappear.
Allah inherits what the boastful person claims and that person comes to Him alone, another separation of the departing human from retained possessions.
